title: Education How to Read Twice as Much Cauthen, Colton
author: Cauthen, Colton
summary: Colton Cauthen addresses the reading FOMO many serious learners experience -- the growing gap between books they want to read and books they actually read -- and offers a two-pronged framework for reading more without anxiety. The first and most counterintuitive lever is extending the time horizon over which you plan your reading: instead of thinking about what to read this year, think across 2-3 years, which immediately makes the quantity of good books feel manageable rather than overwhelming. The second lever is reading multiple books simultaneously in different formats -- one physical book at home, one ebook for travel, one audiobook for commuting -- which creates dedicated reading slots that don't compete with each other. Cauthen also addresses the quality dimension: reading twice as much does not mean reading everything at the same depth, and a tiered approach is not intellectual laziness but realistic information management.
points: The single highest-leverage change for overwhelmed readers is extending the planning time horizon: a two-year reading plan reveals that the gap between 'books to read' and 'books readable in a lifetime' is smaller than annual anxiety makes it feel.

Reading multiple books simultaneously in different formats -- physical, ebook, audio -- creates parallel reading slots that don't compete for the same attention window, effectively multiplying available reading time without requiring more discipline.

Reading anxiety is primarily a comparison problem: people feel behind relative to an implicit standard of what a serious reader should have read, not relative to their own genuine learning needs -- reorienting to personal utility dissolves most of it.

A tiered reading approach -- some books read fully and annotated, others sampled for key chapters, others skimmed for main arguments -- is information management appropriate to a world where worthwhile books vastly exceed any individual's reading capacity.

The goal Cauthen advocates is not speed but volume: slower, more deliberate reading of the right books, chosen for genuine relevance, produces more durable learning than fast reading of more books chosen under FOMO pressure.
quotes: Three years ago, my journal entry for the day expressed an increasing feeling of being overwhelmed by the amount of content-- books especially-- that I wanted to be reading but wasn't. The list of books I wanted to read grew at a rate that far outpaced my reading resulting in something like a reading and learning FOMO. I suspect a lot of people feel this way.
